\chapter{Morning}
\label{ch:ml-morning}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say morning in Malayalam with rāvile and hear the night-word hidden inside it.}

Say rāvile, pull rāvŭ 'night' out of it, and place prabhātaṁ beside it as the Sanskrit alternative.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{രാവിലെ}]{\ml{രാവിലെ} (rāvile) — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} built from \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C26-raavile}



\begin{quote}
Kannada's morning word means \textquotedblleft{}the shining.\textquotedblright{} Telugu's means \textquotedblleft{}rise.\textquotedblright{} Malayalam's most common morning word means something stranger on its face: night.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{രാവിലെ}} (\textbf{rāvile}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning}\textquotedblright{} — is, per Wiktionary, a compound: \textbf{\ml{രാവ്}} (\emph{rāvŭ}) plus the suffixes \textbf{-il} and \textbf{-e}. Here's the honest surprise: \textbf{\ml{രാവ്}} shares its root — not its exact form — with the word already met in Chapter 24, \textbf{\ml{ഇരവ്}} (\emph{iravŭ}), there a \textbf{literary-register synonym for \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} itself}. Wiktionary confirms both as cognates, both tracing to \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} \emph{\textbf{*cira}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{darkness}\textquotedblright{}) — a cognate doublet within Malayalam, not literally one word in two spellings. So Malayalam's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} is, transparently, built from \textbf{night} plus locative-ish suffixes — not from light, dawn, or rising, the strategies Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ}} (\textquotedblleft{}the shining\textquotedblright{}) and Telugu's \textbf{\te{ఉదయం}} (Sanskrit \textquotedblleft{}rise\textquotedblright{}) both reach for instead.

\begin{culture}
No source spells out \textbf{why} \textquotedblleft{}at/in the night\textquotedblright{} came to mean \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} specifically — it's a plausible semantic path (perhaps \textquotedblleft{}the night just ending,\textquotedblright{} the pre-dawn hours) rather than one directly documented step by step. Treat the \textbf{morphological composition} as confirmed (Wiktionary is explicit about the rāvŭ+il+e breakdown); treat the \textbf{semantic mechanism} as a reasonable but unconfirmed inference, not a settled fact.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Malayalam keeps two other words for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} too. \textbf{\ml{പ്രഭാതം}} (\emph{prabhātaṁ}) is a Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama} sharing its root — \textbf{prabhāta}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine, become bright\textquotedblright{} — with Telugu's own \textbf{\te{సుప్రభాతం}} (\emph{suprabhātam}, Telugu's own morning greeting) — a genuine cross-language echo. \textbf{\ml{പുലർച്ച}} (\emph{pulaṟcca}) is native Dravidian, but be honest about its etymology: one database entry links it to a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to subsist, live,\textquotedblright{} which may or may not be the same root behind its \textquotedblleft{}dawn\textquotedblright{} sense — treat that specific connection as unconfirmed, not settled.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rāvile\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} built from rāvŭ (\textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}) + locative suffixes
  \item the honest surprise — a cognate doublet of the night-word already met as iravŭ (Chapter 24), same root, now doing morning's job
  \item prabhātaṁ — same Sanskrit root as Telugu's suprabhātam
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \ml{രാവിലെ} literally built from? (\textbf{\ml{രാവ്}} — \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} — plus locative suffixes -il/-e; a cognate doublet, same root, as \ml{ഇരവ്} met in Chapter 24 — not literally the same word.) Is the exact reason \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} came to mean \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} fully documented? (\textbf{No} — the compound itself is confirmed, but the semantic shift is a plausible, unconfirmed inference.) What root does \ml{പ്രഭാതം} share with Telugu's \te{సుప్రభాతం}? (\textbf{prabhāta} — the same root behind Telugu's \te{సుప్రభాతం}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
